name: Read and say a two-digit numeral
description: Student can read a written two-digit numeral to 120 and say its number name correctly.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown the numeral 47 on a card, the student says 'forty-seven'.
commonError: Student reverses teen numbers, reading 14 as 'forty-one', or reads each digit separately ('four, seven').
checkpointTask: Show eight numeral cards including teens (13, 15) and others (47, 90, 108). Ask the student to read each aloud.

name: Write a numeral to 120 from its name
description: Student can write the correct numeral when a number to 120 is said aloud.
exampleOfSuccess: Hearing 'eighty-three', the student writes 83.
commonError: Student writes teen numbers reversed (writes 41 for 'fourteen'), or writes hundreds literally (1009 for 'one hundred and nine').
checkpointTask: Say six numbers including a teen, a decade and one over 100 (16, 60, 109). Ask the student to write each numeral.

name: Match a numeral to how many
description: Student can match a numeral to a collection or representation showing that many.
exampleOfSuccess: Given the numeral 36 and groups of materials, the student points to the set showing 3 tens and 6 ones.
commonError: Student matches by the first digit only, or counts every object by ones and loses track past 20.
checkpointTask: Lay out three numeral cards and three collections (24, 36, 41). Ask the student to pair each numeral with its quantity.

name: Represent a number with tens and ones
description: Student can show a given two-digit number using grouped materials, such as bundles of ten and single ones or base-10 blocks.
exampleOfSuccess: Asked to show 52, the student sets out 5 ten-bundles and 2 ones.
commonError: Student lays out the digits as loose counts (5 ones and 2 ones) without grouping into tens.
checkpointTask: Name three numbers (28, 40, 63). Ask the student to build each with bundling sticks or base-10 blocks.

name: Place a number on a number line or track
description: Student can place or locate a number to 120 on a number line, number track or hundreds chart.
exampleOfSuccess: Given a 0 to 120 track, the student points near 75 and explains it is past the halfway point.
commonError: Student counts every space from zero each time, or ignores the scale and places by guess.
checkpointTask: Provide a number track and a hundreds chart. Ask the student to find 58, then 90, on each.

name: Order numbers to 120
description: Student can order a set of numbers to 120 from smallest to largest.
exampleOfSuccess: Given cards 19, 91, 13, 31, the student arranges them 13, 19, 31, 91.
commonError: Student orders by first digit only (places 91 before 19), or by the digit that looks bigger.
checkpointTask: Give five mixed cards including a teen-and-reverse pair (17, 71). Ask the student to order them smallest to largest.

name: Say the number before and after, across tens
description: Student can say the number just before and just after a given number to 120, including across tens and hundreds boundaries.
exampleOfSuccess: Asked what comes after 79, the student says 80; after 99, says 100.
commonError: Student says 'seventy-ten' after 79, or cannot cross the boundary at 100.
checkpointTask: Ask for before and after of four numbers chosen at boundaries (30, 79, 100, 120).
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor candidate: connects to AC9M1N03 (skip counting and decade boundaries). Teacher may link after review.

name: Split a number to 10 into two parts
description: Student can split a quantity up to 10 into two parts and name both parts (part-part-whole).
exampleOfSuccess: Given 7 counters, the student separates them into 4 and 3 and says 'four and three make seven'.
commonError: Student names only one part, or the two parts do not recombine to the whole.
checkpointTask: Give the student 6, then 9 counters. Ask them to break each into two parts and name both parts.

name: Show different ways to make a number to 10
description: Student can show more than one way to split the same number to 10 into two parts.
exampleOfSuccess: For 8, the student shows 7 and 1, then 5 and 3, then 4 and 4.
commonError: Student repeats the same split with the parts swapped and counts it as a new way (4 and 3, then 3 and 4).
checkpointTask: Ask the student to find at least three different ways to make 8 with two parts, using counters.

name: Partition a two-digit number into tens and ones
description: Student can partition a two-digit number into its tens and ones using materials and words.
exampleOfSuccess: For 24, the student makes 2 tens and 4 ones and says '24 is 20 and 4'.
commonError: Student treats the digits as separate small numbers (2 and 4) rather than 20 and 4.
checkpointTask: Name three two-digit numbers (31, 47, 60). Ask the student to partition each into tens and ones.

name: Partition a two-digit number more than one way
description: Student can partition a two-digit number in more than one way, beyond just tens and ones.
exampleOfSuccess: For 24, the student shows 20 and 4, then 10 and 14, then 12 and 12.
commonError: Student can only give the tens-and-ones split and treats other partitions as wrong.
checkpointTask: Ask the student to find two different ways to partition 35 using materials, then say each as a number sentence.

name: Unbundle a ten into ten ones
description: Student can show that one ten can be regrouped as ten ones, keeping the number the same.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown 24 as 2 tens and 4 ones, the student unbundles one ten to make 1 ten and 14 ones, and agrees it is still 24.
commonError: Student thinks unbundling changes the total, or loses count of the loose ones.
checkpointTask: Give the student 30 built as 3 tens. Ask them to remake it as 2 tens and some ones, and confirm it is still 30.

name: Find the missing part of a partition
description: Student can find the missing part when a whole and one part are given.
exampleOfSuccess: Told '24 is 20 and what?', the student says 4; told '24 is 10 and what?', says 14.
commonError: Student adds the two given numbers instead of finding the missing part.
checkpointTask: Pose three missing-part questions for 24 (20 and __, 14 and __, 6 and __).
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor candidate: underpins part-part-whole strategies in AC9M1N04. Teacher may link after review.

name: Skip count by tens to 120
description: Student can skip count forwards by tens to at least 120.
exampleOfSuccess: Starting at 10, the student counts 10, 20, 30 and continues past 100 to 120.
commonError: Student stalls at the hundred boundary, saying 'ninety, hundred, hundred-ten'.
checkpointTask: Ask the student to skip count by tens from 10 as far as they can, listening across 100.

name: Skip count by fives
description: Student can skip count forwards by fives.
exampleOfSuccess: The student counts 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and keeps the rhythm.
commonError: Student drifts into counting by ones, or mixes the fives sequence with tens.
checkpointTask: Ask the student to skip count by fives from 5 to at least 60.

name: Skip count by twos
description: Student can skip count forwards by twos.
exampleOfSuccess: The student counts 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and continues.
commonError: Student says odd numbers in between, or restarts from 2 when they lose track.
checkpointTask: Ask the student to skip count by twos from 2 to at least 30.

name: Make equal groups of ten to count
description: Student can organise a large collection into equal groups of ten to make counting easier.
exampleOfSuccess: Given a pile of about 60 counters, the student makes groups of ten before counting.
commonError: Student makes groups of unequal size, or starts counting by ones without grouping.
checkpointTask: Give the student a collection of 40 to 80 objects. Ask them to group it so it is easy to count.

name: Count the groups by skip counting
description: Student can find how many altogether by skip counting equal groups and adding any leftover ones.
exampleOfSuccess: With 6 groups of ten and 3 left over, the student counts 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, then 61, 62, 63.
commonError: Student counts the number of groups (says 6) rather than how many objects, or forgets the leftovers.
checkpointTask: Set out 5 groups of ten and 4 single counters. Ask the student how many there are altogether.

name: Choose a grouping to count efficiently
description: Student can choose to group in tens or fives to count a large collection more efficiently than counting by ones, and say why.
exampleOfSuccess: Faced with a jar of about 80 coins, the student stacks them in tens and explains it is faster and easier to keep track.
commonError: Student insists on counting by ones, or chooses a group size that does not skip count easily (such as threes).
checkpointTask: Show a collection of about 100 objects. Ask the student how they would count it quickly and to explain their choice.

name: Add within 10 with materials
description: Student can add two numbers within 10 using objects, fingers or drawings.
exampleOfSuccess: For 4 + 3, the student sets out 4 then 3 counters and counts 7 altogether.
commonError: Student recounts the first group instead of combining, or miscounts by starting at zero on the last object.
checkpointTask: Pose three additions within 10 (4 + 3, 6 + 2, 5 + 5). Ask the student to solve each with counters.

name: Subtract within 10 with materials
description: Student can subtract within 10 using objects or drawings by taking away.
exampleOfSuccess: For 9 - 4, the student sets out 9 counters, removes 4, and counts 5 left.
commonError: Student removes the wrong amount, or counts the removed group as the answer.
checkpointTask: Pose three subtractions within 10 (9 - 4, 7 - 2, 10 - 6). Ask the student to solve each with counters.

name: Add by counting on from the larger number
description: Student can add by starting at the larger number and counting on, rather than counting from one.
exampleOfSuccess: For 8 + 3, the student says '8 ... 9, 10, 11' and answers 11.
commonError: Student counts on from the first number even when it is smaller (3 + 8 counted from 3), or counts on starting from the larger number itself ('8, 9, 10').
checkpointTask: Pose 8 + 3, then 2 + 7. Ask the student to solve each by counting on, and watch where they start.

name: Subtract by counting back
description: Student can subtract a small number by counting back from the larger number.
exampleOfSuccess: For 11 - 3, the student says '11 ... 10, 9, 8' and answers 8.
commonError: Student counts back including the starting number ('11, 10, 9'), giving 9, or loses track of how many steps to count.
checkpointTask: Pose 12 - 3 and 15 - 2. Ask the student to solve each by counting back.

name: Use number bonds to 10
description: Student can use known part-part-whole facts to 10 to help add or subtract.
exampleOfSuccess: Asked 10 - 6, the student answers 4 quickly, using that 6 and 4 make 10.
commonError: Student recounts from materials every time rather than recalling bonds, showing the facts are not yet known.
checkpointTask: Ask the bonds of 10 quickfire (7 and __, 3 and __, 8 and __) and listen for recall rather than counting.

name: Add through ten (make ten)
description: Student can add within 20 by bridging through ten, splitting the second number to make ten first.
exampleOfSuccess: For 8 + 5, the student says '8 and 2 makes 10, then 3 more is 13'.
commonError: Student adds the ones without bridging and miscounts (gives 12 for 8 + 5), or cannot split the second number usefully.
checkpointTask: Pose 8 + 5 and 9 + 4. Ask the student to solve each by making ten first, and explain the steps.
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor candidate: relies on partitioning from AC9M1N02. Teacher may link after review.

name: Subtract within 20 using a chosen strategy
description: Student can subtract within 20 by choosing a sensible strategy and explaining it.
exampleOfSuccess: For 15 - 6, the student counts back, or bridges down through ten (15 - 5 is 10, then 1 more is 9).
commonError: Student always counts back by ones even when bridging would be easier, or chooses a strategy that does not fit the numbers.
checkpointTask: Pose 15 - 6 and 13 - 4. Ask the student to solve each and explain the strategy they used.

name: Show an additive story with materials
description: Student can represent a simple addition or subtraction story problem using objects or a drawing.
exampleOfSuccess: For 'Sam had 5 shells and found 3 more', the student sets out 5 then adds 3 counters.
commonError: Student represents only one quantity from the story, or draws unrelated pictures.
checkpointTask: Tell a short join story and a short take-away story. Ask the student to show each with counters or a drawing.

name: Decide whether to add or subtract
description: Student can decide whether a practical problem needs adding or taking away.
exampleOfSuccess: Hearing 'There were 8 birds and 3 flew away, how many now?', the student chooses to take away.
commonError: Student adds whenever two numbers appear, regardless of whether the story joins or separates.
checkpointTask: Tell four short problems (two join, two separate). Ask the student to say add or take away for each.

name: Solve an additive problem and answer in context
description: Student can solve a practical addition or subtraction problem to 20 and state the answer in the words of the story.
exampleOfSuccess: For 'There are 9 apples and 6 are eaten', the student works out 3 and says '3 apples are left'.
commonError: Student gives a bare number with no unit, or solves with the wrong operation.
checkpointTask: Pose two story problems to 20. Ask the student to solve each and answer in a full phrase.

name: Model a whole-dollar money problem
description: Student can model an addition or subtraction problem involving whole-dollar amounts.
exampleOfSuccess: For 'A drink costs $4 and a snack costs $5, how much together?', the student combines to $9.
commonError: Student ignores the dollars and treats the numbers as plain counts, or cannot connect coins or notes to the amounts.
checkpointTask: Pose a buying problem and a change problem in whole dollars. Ask the student to model and solve each.

name: Explain how the model matches the story
description: Student can show their thinking with a diagram or materials and explain how it matches the problem.
exampleOfSuccess: The student points to their drawing and says which part is the shells Sam had and which part is the shells he found.
commonError: Student produces an answer but cannot say how their materials or drawing relate to the story.
checkpointTask: After the student solves a story problem, ask them to explain how each part of their model matches the story.

name: Share a collection into equal groups
description: Student can share a collection equally between a given number of groups, dealing one at a time.
exampleOfSuccess: Sharing 12 counters between 3 children, the student deals one to each in turn until none are left, giving 4 each.
commonError: Student shares unevenly, or stops before all items are dealt out.
checkpointTask: Give 12 counters and 3 plates. Ask the student to share them equally and check each plate.

name: Make equal groups of a set size
description: Student can make equal groups of a given size from a collection.
exampleOfSuccess: Asked to make groups of 5 from 15 counters, the student makes 3 groups of 5.
commonError: Student makes groups of different sizes, or includes a leftover in a group to avoid a remainder.
checkpointTask: Give 20 counters. Ask the student to make groups of 4 and say how many groups they made.

name: Solve an equal-sharing problem
description: Student can solve a practical equal-sharing problem and say how many each share gets.
exampleOfSuccess: For 'Share 10 stickers between 2 friends', the student models it and says '5 each'.
commonError: Student counts the total or the number of groups rather than how many per share.
checkpointTask: Pose two sharing stories (10 between 2, 12 between 4). Ask how many each gets.

name: Solve an equal-grouping problem
description: Student can solve a practical equal-grouping problem and say how many groups are made.
exampleOfSuccess: For 'How many teams of 5 from 15 children?', the student models it and says 3 teams.
commonError: Student answers how many in each group instead of how many groups.
checkpointTask: Pose two grouping stories (15 in fives, 12 in threes). Ask how many groups.

name: Notice and describe leftovers
description: Student can recognise and describe when a collection cannot be shared or grouped equally, and what is left over.
exampleOfSuccess: Sharing 13 between 2, the student gives 6 each and says one is left over.
commonError: Student forces an even share by ignoring the extra, or splits an item without acknowledging the remainder.
checkpointTask: Pose a share that does not work out evenly (13 between 2). Ask the student what happens to the extra.

name: Model an equal-sharing money problem
description: Student can model and explain an equal-sharing problem involving money.
exampleOfSuccess: For 'Share $12 equally between 3 people', the student shares to $4 each and explains the model.
commonError: Student shares the number of coins rather than the value, or cannot explain how the model fits the story.
checkpointTask: Pose an equal-sharing money problem in whole dollars. Ask the student to model, solve and explain it.
